title: Τεῖχος καὶ τάφρος
titleEn: The Wall and the Ditch — Iliad 12.1–87
about: Patroclus is still tending Eurypylus in the hut while Argives and Trojans fight on. The poet steps aside to say that the wall and ditch the Achaeans built to protect their ships were raised without sacrifice and against the will of the gods, so that they would stand only while Hector lived, Achilles kept up his wrath and Priam’s city was unsacked. After Troy fell, Poseidon and Apollo would turn the rivers of Ida on the wall for nine days, with Zeus raining, and wipe it away into the sand. Back in the present, the Trojans press the wall and the Argives, beaten down by Zeus’ scourge, cower at the ships. Hector charges about like a boar or lion among hunters, but his horses balk at the ditch, with its sheer banks and sharp stakes. Polydamas advises Hector that horsemen cannot fight there, and that the Trojans should leave the horses with their attendants and go forward on foot in a close mass. Hector likes the advice, leaps down, and the other Trojans follow him, each man telling his charioteer to hold the horses at the ditch, and they form up in five divisions behind their leaders.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ μὲν ἐν κλισίῃσι Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱὸς
ἰᾶτ’ Εὐρύπυλον βεβλημένον· οἳ δὲ μάχοντο
Ἀργεῖοι καὶ Τρῶες ὁμιλαδόν·
sentences.i: So Menoetius’ sturdy son was in the huts healing the wounded Eurypylus; and the Argives and the Trojans fought in a throng;
sentences.n: The book opens on the thread the last part left, Patroclus in Eurypylus’ hut (11.848), and then turns to the fighting. Menoetius’ sturdy son is Patroclus, not named here; ὃ μέν is the pronoun ‘he’ (‘he, for his part’), answered by οἳ δέ ‘and they’ in the next line. ἄλκιμος ‘sturdy’ is the house rendering of the stock epithet. κλισίῃσι is the epic dative plural (Attic κλισίαις). ἰᾶτ’ is ἰᾶτο with the vowel elided, the imperfect middle of ἰάομαι ‘heal’. βεβλημένον is the perfect passive participle of βάλλω: ‘struck’ in the literal line, ‘wounded’ in the free one. μάχοντο is an unaugmented imperfect of μάχομαι ‘fight’. ὁμιλαδόν is built on ὅμιλος ‘throng’ with the adverb ending -δόν, ‘in a throng’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλε
τάφρος ἔτι σχήσειν Δαναῶν καὶ τεῖχος ὕπερθεν
εὐρύ, τὸ ποιήσαντο νεῶν ὕπερ, ἀμφὶ δὲ τάφρον
ἤλασαν·
sentences.l:
And not, then, was destined
the ditch of the Danaans any longer to hold out, and the wall above it,
wide, which they made above the ships, and around it a ditch
they drove;
sentences.i: And the ditch of the Danaans, as it turned out, was no longer going to hold out, nor the wide wall above it, which they had made to shield the ships; and they had driven a ditch around it;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 3 and is the poet speaking in his own voice about the wall and ditch the Achaeans built at 7.433–441. οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλε ‘and, as it turned out, was not going to’ takes the future infinitive σχήσειν, of ἔχω, here used without an object to mean ‘hold out’. The subject is τάφρος ‘ditch’, with καὶ τεῖχος … εὐρύ ‘and the wide wall’ added after it, so the verb is singular. ὕπερθεν is ‘above, on top’. τό is the relative ‘which’, ποιήσαντο the aorist middle of ποιέω, ‘they made for themselves’, and νεῶν ὕπερ ‘above the ships’ means standing over them to shield them. ἀμφὶ δὲ τάφρον ἤλασαν is ‘and around it they drove a ditch’: ἐλαύνω of a ditch is ‘drive’, the line carried across the ground. The words νεῶν ὕπερ, ἀμφὶ δὲ τάφρον ἤλασαν are those of 7.449–450, and their English is kept.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ θεοῖσι δόσαν κλειτὰς ἑκατόμβας·
ὄφρά σφιν νῆάς τε θοὰς καὶ ληΐδα πολλὴν
ἐντὸς ἔχον ῥύοιτο·
sentences.i: and they had not given the gods famous hecatombs, so that the wall might protect for them the swift ships and the plentiful spoil it held within;
sentences.n: The English of the first half-line is that of 7.450 (‘famous hecatombs’, with the tense put into the past; a hecatomb is properly a hundred oxen). The sense is that the work was done without the sacrifice that would have put the gods behind it. δόσαν is an unaugmented aorist (= ἔδοσαν). ὄφρά σφιν … ῥύοιτο is a purpose clause: ὄφρα with the optative ῥύοιτο, of ῥύομαι ‘protect’, after a past tense. The subject, the wall, is not repeated; ἔχον is the neuter participle ‘holding’ agreeing with it, and ἐντός ‘within’ goes with it. νῆας … θοάς is ‘the swift ships’, the stock epithet translated; ληΐδα is ‘spoil’, and σφιν ‘for them’ is the dative of the Achaeans, who benefit.

sentences.t:
θεῶν δ’ ἀέκητι τέτυκτο
ἀθανάτων· τὸ καὶ οὔ τι πολὺν χρόνον ἔμπεδον ἦεν.
sentences.l:
and against the will of the gods it had been made,
the immortals’; for that reason also not much time firm it was.
sentences.i: And it had been made against the will of the immortal gods; so for that reason it did not stay firm for long.
sentences.n: The poet gives the reason the wall fell: the gods had not agreed to it. θεῶν δ’ ἀέκητι is ‘against the will of the gods’ (ἀέκητι takes the genitive), and ἀθανάτων ‘of the immortals’ is held over to the next line. τέτυκτο is the third person singular pluperfect passive of τεύχω, ‘had been made’. τὸ καί is ‘and for that reason’, τό being the neuter used as an adverb. πολὺν χρόνον is ‘for a long time’ (accusative of duration), and ἦεν is a Homeric form of the imperfect of εἰμί (Attic ἦν). ἔμπεδος is ‘firm’, and it returns three lines later.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν Ἕκτωρ ζωὸς ἔην καὶ μήνι’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
καὶ Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος ἀπόρθητος πόλις ἔπλεν,
τόφρα δὲ καὶ μέγα τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν ἔμπεδον ἦεν.
sentences.l:
As long as Hector alive was, and was wrathful Achilles,
and of Priam the lord unsacked the city was,
so long also the great wall of the Achaeans firm was.
sentences.i: As long as Hector was alive and Achilles kept up his wrath, and the city of lord Priam was unsacked, so long the great wall of the Achaeans also stood firm.
sentences.n: ὄφρα μέν … τόφρα δέ is the pair ‘as long as … for so long’, and the whole sentence says that the wall is tied to three things: Hector alive, Achilles in his wrath, Priam’s city whole. ζωὸς ἔην is ‘was alive’ (ἔην = ἦν). μήνι’ is the unaugmented imperfect of μηνίω ‘be wrathful, nurse one’s wrath’, the verb of μῆνις, the poem’s first word. ἄνακτος ‘lord’ is the house rendering of ἄναξ. ἀπόρθητος ‘unsacked’ has the same root as πέρθετο ‘was sacked’ four lines below. ἔπλεν is ἔπλετο ‘was’. ἔμπεδον ἦεν ‘was firm’ repeats line 9, with ‘firm’ in the same sense.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατὰ μὲν Τρώων θάνον ὅσσοι ἄριστοι,
πολλοὶ δ’ Ἀργείων οἳ μὲν δάμεν, οἳ δὲ λίποντο,
πέρθετο δὲ Πριάμοιο πόλις δεκάτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ,
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ἐν νηυσὶ φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἔβησαν,
sentences.l:
But when, of the Trojans, had died all who were best,
and of the Argives many, some were overcome, and some were left,
and was sacked the city of Priam in the tenth year,
and the Argives in ships to their dear fatherland went,
sentences.i: But when all the best of the Trojans had died, and of the Argives many, some overcome and some left, and the city of Priam had been sacked in the tenth year, and the Argives had gone in their ships to their dear fatherland,
sentences.n: From here to line 33 the poet looks past the end of the war. This is a long clause of time that waits for its main clause, δὴ τότε in the next unit, so the unit ends at a comma. κατὰ … θάνον is tmesis for κατέθανον: θάνον is the unaugmented aorist of θνῄσκω, ‘died’. ὅσσοι ἄριστοι is ‘as many as were best’. In οἳ μὲν δάμεν, οἳ δὲ λίποντο, οἳ μέν … οἳ δέ are ‘some … others’, pronouns and not relatives; δάμεν is the aorist passive of δάμνημι ‘overcome’ (epic -εν for -ησαν), and λίποντο is the aorist middle of λείπω used passively, ‘were left behind’, that is, survived. πέρθετο is a middle form of πέρθω ‘sack’ with passive sense, ‘was sacked’; its stem is the present stem πέρθ- (the aorist stem is πραθ-), so formally it is an unaugmented imperfect, here standing for a single past event. δεκάτῳ ἐνιαυτῷ is a dative of time, ‘in the tenth year’. φίλην … πατρίδ’ is ‘dear fatherland’ with γαῖαν left to be understood, as in the house phrase φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε μητιόωντο Ποσειδάων καὶ Ἀπόλλων
τεῖχος ἀμαλδῦναι ποταμῶν μένος εἰσαγαγόντες.
sentences.l:
then indeed devised Poseidon and Apollo
the wall to wipe out, the might of rivers bringing in.
sentences.i: then Poseidon and Apollo planned to wipe out the wall, bringing in the might of the rivers.
sentences.n: This is the main clause the last unit was waiting for. δὴ τότε is ‘then indeed’. μητιόωντο is the imperfect of μητιάομαι ‘plan, devise’, uncontracted (Attic ἐμητιῶντο), and it takes the aorist infinitive ἀμαλδῦναι of ἀμαλδύνω ‘wear away, wipe out’. ποταμῶν μένος is ‘the might of the rivers’; μένος is the house ‘might’. εἰσαγαγόντες is the aorist participle of εἰσάγω ‘bring in’, with the two gods as subject. The next unit names the rivers.

sentences.t:
ὅσσοι ἀπ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων ἅλα δὲ προρέουσι,
Ῥῆσός θ’ Ἑπτάπορός τε Κάρησός τε Ῥοδίος τε
Γρήνικός τε καὶ Αἴσηπος δῖός τε Σκάμανδρος
καὶ Σιμόεις, ὅθι πολλὰ βοάγρια καὶ τρυφάλειαι
κάππεσον ἐν κονίῃσι καὶ ἡμιθέων γένος ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l:
all that from the Idaean mountains to the sea flow forth,
Rhesus and Heptaporus and Caresus and Rhodius
and Granicus and Aesepus and heavenly Scamander
and the Simois, where many ox-hide shields and helms
fell in the dust, and the race of men half-divine;
sentences.i: all those that flow forth to the sea from the mountains of Ida: the Rhesus, the Heptaporus, the Caresus, the Rhodius, the Granicus, the Aesepus, and heavenly Scamander, and the Simois, where many ox-hide shields and helmets fell in the dust, and the race of men who were half gods;
sentences.n: A relative clause that tells which rivers are meant, ποταμῶν in line 18. ὅσσοι is ‘as many as’. ἅλα δέ is read as ἅλαδε ‘to the sea’, the -δε of motion written as two words in the edition. προρέουσι is Attic προρρέουσι, ‘flow forth’. The poet names eight rivers. δῖος is the stock ‘heavenly’, here of the Scamander. βοάγρια is a rare word whose meaning is not known; ‘ox-hide shields’ is the traditional guess. τρυφάλειαι ‘helms’ is another word of unknown derivation (a kind of helmet). κάππεσον is κατέπεσον (aorist of καταπίπτω ‘fall down’) with the τ assimilated to the π, and κονίῃσι is the epic dative plural of κονίη ‘dust’. ἡμιθέων … ἀνδρῶν ‘of men half-divine’ is the poet’s name for the heroes of the war.

sentences.t:
τῶν πάντων ὁμόσε στόματ’ ἔτραπε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
ἐννῆμαρ δ’ ἐς τεῖχος ἵει ῥόον·
sentences.l:
of all of them to the same place the mouths turned Phoebus Apollo,
and for nine days against the wall he sent the flood;
sentences.i: Phoebus Apollo turned the mouths of all of them to one place, and for nine days sent their flood against the wall;
sentences.n: Apollo does the first part of the work. τῶν πάντων is ‘of all of them’, the rivers. ὁμόσε is ‘to the same place’, and στόματα ‘mouths’ are the river-mouths; the sense is that all of them were turned to run against the wall. ἔτραπε is the aorist of τρέπω ‘turn’. ἐννῆμαρ is ‘for nine days’. ἵει is the imperfect of ἵημι ‘send’, and ῥόον is the accusative of ῥόος ‘stream, flow’. Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is ‘Phoebus Apollo’ as always.

sentences.t:
ὗε δ’ ἄρα Ζεὺς
συνεχές, ὄφρά κε θᾶσσον ἁλίπλοα τείχεα θείη.
sentences.l:
and Zeus rained
continuously, so that the sooner sea-sailed he might make the walls.
sentences.i: and Zeus rained without a break, so that he might the sooner make the walls sea-washed.
sentences.n: ὗε is the imperfect of ὕω ‘rain’ and συνεχές is the adverb ‘continuously’, set at the start of line 26. The purpose clause is ὄφρά κε with the optative θείη (aorist optative of τίθημι), ‘so that he might make’. τείχεα is a plural for the one wall. ἁλίπλοα is a rare word, built on ἅλς ‘sea’ and πλέω ‘sail, float’; its exact sense is not certain. ‘Sea-sailed’ is the literal version of the two parts, and ‘sea-washed’ in the free line is the sense most often given, the walls lying under the sea’s reach. Poseidon takes his part in the next unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐννοσίγαιος ἔχων χείρεσσι τρίαιναν
ἡγεῖτ’, ἐκ δ’ ἄρα πάντα θεμείλια κύμασι πέμπε
φιτρῶν καὶ λάων, τὰ θέσαν μογέοντες Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.l:
and himself the earth-shaker, holding in his hands the trident,
led the way, and out all the foundations to the waves he sent,
of logs and stones, which had laid, toiling, the Achaeans,
sentences.i: And the earth-shaker himself, holding the trident in his hands, led the way and sent all the foundations, of logs and stones, which the Achaeans had laid with toil, out into the waves,
sentences.n: Poseidon has been named at line 17, so the bare ἐννοσίγαιος ‘earth-shaker’ is enough; αὐτός ‘himself’ stresses that he took the lead. ἔχων χείρεσσι τρίαιναν is ‘holding the trident in his hands’ (χείρεσσι is the epic dative plural of χείρ). ἡγεῖτ’ is ἡγεῖτο, the imperfect of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’. ἐκ … πέμπε is tmesis for ἐξέπεμπε ‘sent out’. θεμείλια are ‘foundations’, and φιτρῶν καὶ λάων ‘of logs and stones’ says what they were made of; λάων is the genitive plural of λᾶας ‘stone’, not a form of the verb λάω. θέσαν is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι (= ἔθεσαν), ‘laid, put down’, and μογέοντες is the uncontracted participle of μογέω ‘toil’.

sentences.t:
λεῖα δ’ ἐποίησεν παρ’ ἀγάρροον Ἑλλήσποντον,
αὖτις δ’ ἠϊόνα μεγάλην ψαμάθοισι κάλυψε
τεῖχος ἀμαλδύνας·
sentences.i: and made them smooth along the strong-flowing Hellespont, and covered the great beach over again with sands, once he had wiped out the wall;
sentences.n: λεῖα ‘smooth’ is a neuter plural complement: he ‘made them smooth’, the foundations being the things made level. ἀγάρροον is the stock ‘strong-flowing’, used of the Hellespont, the strait along which the Achaean ships were drawn up. αὖτις is ‘again’. ἠϊόνα μεγάλην ψαμάθοισι κάλυψε has the same words as 7.462, there with the infinitive καλύψαι; here it is done. ψαμάθοισι is the plural ‘sands’. κάλυψε is an unaugmented aorist, and ἀμαλδύνας is the aorist participle of the verb of line 18, ‘having wiped out’.

sentences.t:
ποταμοὺς δ’ ἔτρεψε νέεσθαι
κὰρ ῥόον, ᾗ περ πρόσθεν ἵεν καλλίρροον ὕδωρ.
sentences.l:
and the rivers he turned to go back
down the stream, just where before they sent their fair-flowing water.
sentences.i: and turned the rivers back to flow down their stream, just where before they had sent their fair-flowing water.
sentences.n: The rivers are put back where they were. ποταμοὺς … νέεσθαι is ‘the rivers … to go’, νέεσθαι being the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι ‘go, go back’. κὰρ ῥόον is κατὰ ῥόον with the τ assimilated to the ρ, ‘down the stream’. ᾗ περ is ‘just where’, and πρόσθεν ‘before’. ἵεν is the imperfect of ἵημι, third person plural (Attic ἵεσαν); the singular ἵει at line 25 is the same verb. καλλίρροον is ‘fair-flowing’, as the house table has it for the same compound elsewhere. The full stop closes the whole look into the future.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔμελλον ὄπισθε Ποσειδάων καὶ Ἀπόλλων
θησέμεναι·
sentences.l:
So, then, were destined, afterwards, Poseidon and Apollo
to bring it about;
sentences.i: So, in later days, Poseidon and Apollo were to bring it about;
sentences.n: A new paragraph of the edition begins here, bringing the poem back from the look ahead. ὣς is ‘so’, summing up the whole account of lines 17–33, and ὄπισθε is ‘afterwards, later’. ἔμελλον ‘were destined’ takes the future infinitive θησέμεναι, the epic form of Attic θήσειν, of τίθημι ‘put, make’; ‘to bring it about’ is the sense here, the object being left unsaid.

sentences.t:
τότε δ’ ἀμφὶ μάχη ἐνοπή τε δεδήει
τεῖχος ἐΰδμητον, κανάχιζε δὲ δούρατα πύργων
βαλλόμεν’·
sentences.i: But at that time the fighting and the shouting blazed around the well-built wall, and the timbers of its towers rang as they were struck;
sentences.n: τότε ‘at that time’ brings us back to the story’s present. ἀμφὶ … τεῖχος ἐΰδμητον is ‘around the well-built wall’, with ἀμφί set before the noun; ἐΰδμητος is the stock ‘well-built’. δεδήει is the pluperfect of δαίω ‘burn’, used with the sense of an imperfect, ‘was ablaze’. ἐνοπή ‘shouting’ is the cry of many men. κανάχιζε is the imperfect of καναχίζω ‘ring, clang’. δούρατα is the plural of δόρυ, which means wood as well as spear; here it is the woodwork of the towers, ‘timbers’, and not spears. βαλλόμεν’ is βαλλόμενα, the neuter plural passive participle agreeing with δούρατα.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δὲ Διὸς μάστιγι δαμέντες
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐελμένοι ἰσχανόωντο
Ἕκτορα δειδιότες, κρατερὸν μήστωρα φόβοιο·
sentences.i: and the Argives, overcome by the whip of Zeus and hemmed in at the hollow ships, held themselves back, in fear of Hector, strong master of flight;
sentences.n: Διὸς μάστιγι is ‘by the whip of Zeus’, the scourge he lays on them; δαμέντες is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘overcome’. ἐελμένοι is the perfect passive participle of εἴλω ‘pen in, hem in’, with the epic doubled ε. νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν is ‘at the hollow ships’, the preposition set after its noun; γλαφυρός is the stock ‘hollow’. ἰσχανόωντο is the imperfect of ἰσχανάομαι ‘hold oneself back’, uncontracted (Attic ἰσχανῶντο). δειδιότες is the perfect participle of δείδω ‘fear’. κρατερὸν μήστωρα φόβοιο is the stock phrase for a master of the rout: μήστωρ is a ‘planner, deviser’ (compare μήδομαι) and φόβος is the flight that fear drives; ‘counsellor’ in the literal line, ‘master’ in the free line, as for the same phrase at 5.272.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ὡς τὸ πρόσθεν ἐμάρνατο ἶσος ἀέλλῃ·
sentences.l: but he, as before, fought, equal to a blast;
sentences.i: but Hector fought as before, like a storm;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns from the Argives to Hector, the ὅ γ’ ‘he’. ἐμάρνατο is the imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’; ὡς τὸ πρόσθεν is ‘as before’, τό being the neuter used as an adverb. ἶσος means ‘equal to’, and ἀέλλῃ is the dative of ἄελλα ‘blast, storm-wind’. The picture of the storm gives way to the longer picture of the beast in the next lines.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἔν τε κύνεσσι καὶ ἀνδράσι θηρευτῇσι
κάπριος ἠὲ λέων στρέφεται σθένεϊ βλεμεαίνων·
sentences.l:
And as when, among both dogs and men, hunters,
a boar or a lion wheels, in strength exulting;
sentences.i: And as when, among dogs and men who hunt, a boar or a lion wheels about, exulting in its strength;
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν … opens a simile, ‘and as when’; ὅτ’ ἄν with a present indicative is the epic way to say ‘whenever’. ἔν τε κύνεσσι καὶ ἀνδράσι θηρευτῇσι is ‘both among dogs and among hunters’, κύνεσσι and θηρευτῇσι being epic datives plural (Attic θηρευταῖς). κάπριος ‘wild boar’ and λέων ‘lion’ are alternatives. στρέφεται is middle, ‘turns itself, wheels about’. σθένεϊ is the dative of σθένος ‘strength’. βλεμεαίνων is rare; ‘exulting’ is the usual guess at its sense, which is not certain. The sentence goes on in the next three units.

sentences.t:
οἳ δέ τε πυργηδὸν σφέας αὐτοὺς ἀρτύναντες
ἀντίον ἵστανται καὶ ἀκοντίζουσι θαμειὰς
αἰχμὰς ἐκ χειρῶν·
sentences.i: and they array themselves like a tower, face it and stand, and hurl spear after spear from their hands in close succession;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ τε is ‘and they’, the men, the hunters, with the epic τε that marks a general truth. πυργηδόν is ‘tower-wise’, ‘like a tower’, an adverb in -δόν like ὁμιλαδόν at line 3; a πύργος can be the figure for a close-packed body of men. ἀρτύναντες is the aorist participle of ἀρτύνω ‘set in order’, and σφέας αὐτούς ‘themselves’ is its object; the same words end line 86. ἀντίον is ‘face to face, against’, ἵστανται ‘take their stand’, ἀκοντίζουσι ‘hurl’. θαμειάς is ‘thick, close-set’, and αἰχμάς ‘spears’. The mid-line stop after χειρῶν ends the unit.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ οὔ ποτε κυδάλιμον κῆρ
ταρβεῖ οὐδὲ φοβεῖται, ἀγηνορίη δέ μιν ἔκτα·
sentences.l:
but of him never the glorious heart
is dismayed nor takes flight, and his manliness kills him;
sentences.i: but the glorious heart of the beast is never dismayed and never takes flight; it is its own manliness that kills it;
sentences.n: τοῦ δ’ ‘but of him’ is the boar or lion, with the beast’s heart as subject. κυδάλιμον is the stock ‘glorious’. ταρβεῖ is the present of ταρβέω ‘be dismayed’, and φοβεῖται is the middle of φοβέω, ‘is put to flight, takes flight’. ἀγηνορίη is ‘manliness’, from ἀνήρ; the word can be praise (courage) or blame (overbearing pride), and the line plays on it. ἔκτα is the strong aorist of κτείνω, here a general statement: ‘kills’. The comparison with Hector carries the same edge, since his daring is what drives him on.

sentences.t:
ταρφέα τε στρέφεται στίχας ἀνδρῶν πειρητίζων·
ὅππῃ τ’ ἰθύσῃ τῇ εἴκουσι στίχες ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l:
and often it wheels, the ranks of men testing;
wherever it rushes, there give way the ranks of men;
sentences.i: and it wheels about again and again, testing the ranks of men; wherever it charges, the ranks of men give way;
sentences.n: ταρφέα is ‘thick, often’, here an adverb. στρέφεται is the same verb as in line 42. πειρητίζων is the participle of πειρητίζω ‘try, test’, an epic form of πειράω. ὅππῃ is the epic form of ὅπῃ ‘wherever’; τ’ is the generalizing τε; ἰθύσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἰθύω ‘rush straight’; τῇ is ‘there’; εἴκουσι is ‘give way’. στίχας ἀνδρῶν (line 47) and στίχες ἀνδρῶν (line 48, at its end), the same words in two cases, are the poet’s own echo: the ranks that the beast tests are the ranks that give way.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἕκτωρ ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἰὼν ἐλλίσσεθ’ ἑταίρους
τάφρον ἐποτρύνων διαβαινέμεν·
sentences.l:
So Hector through the throng going begged his companions,
the ditch urging to cross;
sentences.i: So Hector went through the throng, begging his companions and urging them to cross the ditch;
sentences.n: ὣς Ἕκτωρ picks up the simile: ‘so Hector’, answering ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἄν. ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἰών is ‘going up through the throng’. ἐλλίσσεθ’ is ἐλλίσσετο, the imperfect of ἐλλίσσομαι ‘beg’. ἑταίρους ‘companions’ is the accusative object of both verbs. ἐποτρύνων is the participle of ἐποτρύνω ‘urge on’, and διαβαινέμεν is the epic infinitive (Attic διαβαίνειν) ‘to cross’, governed by both. The next lines say why the crossing is the difficulty.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ οἱ ἵπποι
τόλμων ὠκύποδες, μάλα δὲ χρεμέτιζον ἐπ’ ἄκρῳ
χείλει ἐφεσταότες·
sentences.i: but his swift-footed horses did not dare it; they stood on the very edge and whinnied loudly;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 50. οὐδέ οἱ ἵπποι is ‘and not for him the horses’, οἱ being the dative of the pronoun, Hector’s. τόλμων is the imperfect of τολμάω ‘dare’ (Attic ἐτόλμων). ὠκύποδες ‘swift-footed’ is the stock epithet and is translated here though the horses are balking. χρεμέτιζον is the imperfect of χρεμετίζω ‘whinny’. ἐπ’ ἄκρῳ χείλει is ‘on the topmost lip’, the lip being the edge of the ditch. ἐφεσταότες is the perfect participle of ἐφίστημι in its epic form (Attic ἐφεστῶτες), ‘standing upon’.

sentences.t:
ἀπὸ γὰρ δειδίσσετο τάφρος
εὐρεῖ’, οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ὑπερθορέειν σχεδὸν οὔτε περῆσαι
ῥηϊδίη·
sentences.i: for the wide ditch scared them off, being neither easy to leap across from close by nor easy to cross;
sentences.n: The unit begins mid-line. ἀπὸ … δειδίσσετο is tmesis; δειδίσσομαι is the verb of ‘frighten’ (from δείδω), here middle with an active force, and the preverb gives ‘scared them off’. The subject is τάφρος ‘the ditch’, with εὐρεῖ’, elided εὐρεῖα, ‘wide’. οὔτ’ … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’, with the infinitives ὑπερθορέειν (aorist of ὑπερθρῴσκω, uncontracted) ‘to leap over’ and περῆσαι (aorist of περάω, Attic περᾶσαι) ‘to cross’, and ῥηϊδίη (Attic ῥᾴδιος) ‘easy’ agrees with τάφρος. σχεδόν is ‘near, close at hand’; the exact point of ‘from near’ is not spelled out in the line, and the sense taken here is leaping from right at the edge.

sentences.t:
κρημνοὶ γὰρ ἐπηρεφέες περὶ πᾶσαν
ἕστασαν ἀμφοτέρωθεν, ὕπερθεν δὲ σκολόπεσσιν
ὀξέσιν ἠρήρει, τοὺς ἵστασαν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
πυκνοὺς καὶ μεγάλους δηΐων ἀνδρῶν ἀλεωρήν.
sentences.l:
for banks, overhanging, all along it
stood on either side, and above with stakes
sharp it was fitted, which set up the sons of the Achaeans,
thick and great, a defence from hostile men.
sentences.i: For overhanging banks stood all along it on either side, and along the top it was fitted with sharp stakes, thick and large, which the sons of the Achaeans had set up as a defence against enemy men.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 54. κρημνοί are ‘steep banks, sheer edges’ and ἐπηρεφέες is ‘overhanging’, uncontracted (Attic ἐπηρεφεῖς). ἕστασαν is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘stood’, and ἀμφοτέρωθεν ‘on both sides’. ἠρήρει is the pluperfect of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, with the ditch as the unstated subject; σκολόπεσσιν is the epic dative plural of σκόλοψ ‘stake’. τούς is the relative ‘which’, with ἵστασαν the imperfect of ἵστημι in its transitive sense, ‘set up’; υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘sons of the Achaeans’ means the Achaeans. πυκνοὺς καὶ μεγάλους ‘thick and large’ agrees with the stakes. ἀλεωρήν is ‘a defence’ and δηΐων ἀνδρῶν ‘of hostile men’, δήϊος meaning ‘hostile, of the enemy’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οὔ κεν ῥέα ἵππος ἐΰτροχον ἅρμα τιταίνων
ἐσβαίη, πεζοὶ δὲ μενοίνεον εἰ τελέουσι.
sentences.l:
There not easily would a horse, a well-rolling chariot straining at,
get in, but men on foot were eager if they would accomplish it.
sentences.i: There no horse straining at a well-rolling chariot could easily get in; but the men on foot were eager to see whether they would manage it.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘there’, at the ditch. οὔ κεν … ἐσβαίη is a potential optative, ‘would not get in’, ἐσβαίη being the aorist optative of εἰσβαίνω. ῥέα is ‘easily’ (= ῥεῖα). ἐΰτροχον ‘well-rolling’ is the stock epithet of the chariot, and τιταίνων ‘straining at’ is said of a horse at its load. μενοίνεον is the uncontracted imperfect of μενοινάω ‘be eager, be minded’, and εἰ τελέουσι is ‘whether they would accomplish it’, with an uncontracted future (Attic τελοῦσι). The free line adds ‘to see’, which the Greek leaves out. The sentence prepares Polydamas’ advice.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε Πουλυδάμας θρασὺν Ἕκτορα εἶπε παραστάς·
sentences.l: then indeed Polydamas to bold Hector spoke, standing beside him:
sentences.i: Then Polydamas stood beside bold Hector and spoke:
sentences.n: This sentence leads into the speech that follows in the next unit. δὴ τότε is ‘then indeed’. εἶπε παραστάς is ‘spoke, standing beside’, παραστάς being the aorist participle of παρίστημι. θρασύν is ‘bold’, the narrator’s word for Hector; it is translated every time it comes. The name Πουλυδάμας is Polydamas, who speaks to the war-leader at his side.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ τ’ ἠδ’ ἄλλοι Τρώων ἀγοὶ ἠδ’ ἐπικούρων
ἀφραδέως διὰ τάφρον ἐλαύνομεν ὠκέας ἵππους·
sentences.l:
“Hector, and you other leaders of the Trojans and of the allies,
senselessly through the ditch we are driving our swift horses;
sentences.i: “Hector, and you other leaders of the Trojans and of the allies, we are driving our swift horses senselessly through the ditch;
sentences.n: Polydamas begins at once with a complaint. Ἕκτορ τ’ ἠδ’ ἄλλοι is ‘Hector and the others’: τε … ἠδέ link the two, and ἄλλοι is nominative plural in address. ἀγοί is the nominative plural of ἀγός ‘leader’, and ἐπικούρων is the genitive plural of ἐπίκουρος ‘ally’, the troops who fight for Troy but are not Trojans. ἀφραδέως is ‘senselessly’, from ἀφραδής. ἐλαύνομεν is the present, ‘we are driving’, and ὠκέας ἵππους ‘swift horses’ is the stock phrase.

sentences.t: ἣ δὲ μάλ’ ἀργαλέη περάαν·
sentences.l: and it is very hard to cross;
sentences.i: and it is very hard to cross;
sentences.n: ἣ δέ is ‘and it’, the demonstrative pronoun and not a relative, the ditch being meant. μάλα ‘very’ goes with ἀργαλέη, ‘hard’. περάαν is the uncontracted infinitive of περάω (Attic περᾶν), ‘to cross’. The unit is short because the sentence stops after περάαν, in mid-line.

sentences.t:
σκόλοπες γὰρ ἐν αὐτῇ
ὀξέες ἑστᾶσιν, ποτὶ δ’ αὐτοὺς τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν,
ἔνθ’ οὔ πως ἔστιν καταβήμεναι οὐδὲ μάχεσθαι
ἱππεῦσι·
sentences.l:
for stakes in it
sharp are standing, and right against them the wall of the Achaeans,
where there is no way to go down or to fight
for horsemen;
sentences.i: for sharp stakes stand in it, and right against them the wall of the Achaeans, where there is no way for horsemen to go down or to fight;
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 63. σκόλοπες ὀξέες ἑστᾶσιν is ‘sharp stakes are standing’; ἑστᾶσιν is the perfect of ἵστημι (Attic ἑστᾶσι). ποτὶ δ’ αὐτούς is ‘and right up against them’, ποτί being πρός. ἔνθ’ is ‘there’, in that place, and οὔ πως ἔστιν ‘there is no way’ takes the infinitives καταβήμεναι (aorist, epic -μεναι; ‘to go down’; whether from the chariot or into the ditch the line does not say) and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’, with ἱππεῦσι ‘for horsemen’ as the dative they are said of. The thought is that men in chariots cannot get down or fight in so narrow a place.

sentences.t: στεῖνος γάρ, ὅθι τρώσεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.l: for it is a narrow place, where I think we shall be wounded.
sentences.i: for it is a narrow place, and there, I think, we shall be wounded.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 66. στεῖνος is ‘narrow place, narrowness’, with ‘it is’ understood. ὅθι is ‘where’. τρώσεσθαι is the future infinitive of τιτρώσκω ‘wound’, used as a passive, ‘to be wounded’, and ὀΐω ‘I think’ takes it. Polydamas here speaks of what he expects, not what he knows.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν γὰρ τοὺς πάγχυ κακὰ φρονέων ἀλαπάζει
Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης, Τρώεσσι δὲ ἵετ’ ἀρήγειν,
ἦ τ’ ἂν ἔγωγ’ ἐθέλοιμι καὶ αὐτίκα τοῦτο γενέσθαι,
νωνύμνους ἀπολέσθαι ἀπ’ Ἄργεος ἐνθάδ’ Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l:
For if utterly evils devising these
Zeus the high-thundering is laying waste, and for the Trojans is eager to help,
then indeed I for my part would wish even at once this to happen,
nameless to perish far from Argos here the Achaeans;
sentences.i: For if Zeus who thunders on high is utterly laying them waste, with evil in his mind, and is eager to help the Trojans, then I for one would wish this to happen at once: that the Achaeans perish here, nameless, far from Argos;
sentences.n: A condition with two outcomes, the first given here. εἰ μὲν γάρ … ἦ τ’ ἂν … ἐθέλοιμι is ‘for if … then I would wish’, the optative with ἄν answering the εἰ. τοὺς is the pronoun ‘them’, the Achaeans. πάγχυ is ‘utterly’. κακὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking evils’, with evil in his mind. ἀλαπάζει is ‘lays waste’, as the house table has it. Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης is ‘high-thundering Zeus’, the stock epithet. ἵετ’ is ἵεται, from ἵεμαι ‘be eager’, and takes ἀρήγειν ‘to help’. ἐθέλοιμι ‘I would wish’ takes the accusative and infinitive τοῦτο γενέσθαι. νωνύμνους is ‘nameless’, without a name left behind them, and ἀπ’ Ἄργεος ἐνθάδε ‘here, far from Argos’. If Zeus really means ruin for the Achaeans, Polydamas would see it done now, rather than watch the Trojans lose men to the ditch.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ χ’ ὑποστρέψωσι, παλίωξις δὲ γένηται
ἐκ νηῶν καὶ τάφρῳ ἐνιπλήξωμεν ὀρυκτῇ,
οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτ’ ὀΐω οὐδ’ ἄγγελον ἀπονέεσθαι
ἄψορρον προτὶ ἄστυ ἑλιχθέντων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
but if they turn about, and a chase back come
from the ships, and into the ditch we dash, the dug one,
no longer then I think even a messenger will go back
backwards to the town, having been wheeled round by the Achaeans.
sentences.i: But if they turn around, and a chase back from the ships comes, and we dash into the dug ditch, then I do not think even a messenger will get back to the town, when we have been turned about by the Achaeans.
sentences.n: The other outcome. εἰ δέ χ’ ὑποστρέψωσι is ‘but if they turn around’, χ’ being κε and the aorist subjunctive ὑποστρέψωσι the mood after εἰ κε (= ἐάν); the subject is the Achaeans. παλίωξις is a rare noun for a pursuit turned back on those who pursued; the word is not common enough for its sense to be exactly known. ἐνιπλήξωμεν is the aorist subjunctive of ἐνιπλήσσω ‘strike against, dash into’, and ὀρυκτῇ is ‘dug’ (ὀρύσσω). οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτ’ ὀΐω … ἀπονέεσθαι is ‘I think no longer … will go back’: the English puts the negative on ‘I think’: ‘I do not think’. οὐδ’ ἄγγελον ‘not even a messenger’ is the point: no one would be left to carry the news. ἄψορρον is ‘backwards’, ἄστυ ‘town’. ἑλιχθέντων is the aorist passive participle of ἑλίσσω ‘turn, wheel’, in the genitive absolute, with ‘us’ understood.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω πειθώμεθα πάντες·
sentences.l: But come, as I may say, let us obey, all of us;
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say;
sentences.n: This whole line is already in the poem, and the English is the one it has there. ἄγεθ’ is the plural imperative of ἄγω, ‘come’, ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω ‘as I may say’ has the aorist subjunctive, and πειθώμεθα is the aorist subjunctive middle of πείθομαι, ‘let us obey’. Polydamas turns from the two cases to his plan.

sentences.t:
ἵππους μὲν θεράποντες ἐρυκόντων ἐπὶ τάφρῳ,
αὐτοὶ δὲ πρυλέες σὺν τεύχεσι θωρηχθέντες
Ἕκτορι πάντες ἑπώμεθ’ ἀολλέες·
sentences.i: let the attendants hold the horses back at the ditch, and let us ourselves, the foot-soldiers, armed in our armour, all follow Hector in a close mass;
sentences.n: ἵππους μὲν … αὐτοὶ δέ is ‘the horses … but we ourselves’. ἐρυκόντων is the third person plural present imperative of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, ‘let them hold back’. θεράποντες are ‘attendants’. πρυλέες is the word for fighters on foot, ‘foot-soldiers’. θωρηχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, and σὺν τεύχεσι ‘with the armour’ goes with it; the English of line 77 is the published one with the person changed (they to we). ἑπώμεθ’ is the aorist subjunctive middle of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, again ‘let us’. ἀολλέες is ‘crowded together, in a close mass’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
οὐ μενέουσ’ εἰ δή σφιν ὀλέθρου πείρατ’ ἐφῆπται.
sentences.l:
and the Achaeans
will not stand, if indeed upon them the limits of destruction have been fastened.”
sentences.i: and the Achaeans will not stand their ground, if the limits of destruction have indeed been fastened upon them.”
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 78 and ends Polydamas’ speech. αὐτάρ ‘and then’ introduces what follows from the plan. μενέουσ’ is μενέουσι, the uncontracted future of μένω, ‘will stand their ground’. εἰ δή is ‘if indeed’, and σφιν ‘to them’, ‘upon them’ in the English. ὀλέθρου πείρατ’ ἐφῆπται is ‘the limits of destruction have been fastened on’: πείρατα are ‘ends, limits’, and also the ends of a cord or rope, so the picture may be of a cord with the ends of ruin bound on them; ἐφῆπται is the perfect passive of ἐφάπτω ‘fasten on’, with a singular verb for the neuter plural noun. ‘Limits’ and ‘fastened’ are the words used at 7.402.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο Πουλυδάμας, ἅδε δ’ Ἕκτορι μῦθος ἀπήμων,
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν ἆλτο χαμᾶζε.
sentences.l:
So spoke Polydamas, and it pleased Hector, the word, harmless,
and at once from the chariot, with his armour, he leapt to the ground.
sentences.i: So spoke Polydamas, and his harmless word pleased Hector, and at once he leapt from his chariot to the ground in his armour.
sentences.n: A new paragraph of the edition begins here. ὣς φάτο Πουλυδάμας ‘so spoke Polydamas’ closes the speech; φάτο is the unaugmented aorist of φημί. ἅδε is the unaugmented aorist of ἁνδάνω ‘please’, with the dative Ἕκτορι, and its subject is μῦθος ‘word’, which here means advice. ἀπήμων is ‘harmless’, from πῆμα ‘woe’ with the negative prefix: advice that brings no harm; the house table uses ‘harmless’ for the same word said of a wind. The sentence runs on into line 81, whose English is the one it has elsewhere in the poem: ὀχέων is the plural ὄχεα for the one chariot, ἆλτο the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and χαμᾶζε ‘to the ground’ has the -ζε of motion.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μὲν ἄλλοι Τρῶες ἐφ’ ἵππων ἠγερέθοντο,
ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ πάντες ὄρουσαν, ἐπεὶ ἴδον Ἕκτορα δῖον.
sentences.l:
Nor yet the other Trojans on their horses were gathering,
but off all leapt, when they saw Hector, the heavenly.
sentences.i: Nor did the other Trojans stay massed on their horses; they all leapt down when they saw heavenly Hector.
sentences.n: οὐδὲ μέν is ‘nor yet’. ἐφ’ ἵππων is ‘on horses’; the horses stand for the chariots they draw, and the English keeps ‘horses’. ἠγερέθοντο is the imperfect of ἀγερέθομαι ‘gather together’, here ‘stay gathered, stay massed’. ἀπὸ … ὄρουσαν is tmesis, ‘leapt off’, ὄρουσαν being an unaugmented aorist of ὀρούω, and ἴδον is an unaugmented aorist of ὁράω, ‘saw’. Ἕκτορα δῖον is ‘heavenly Hector’, the stock epithet translated every time. The Trojans do what Hector has just done.

sentences.t:
ἡνιόχῳ μὲν ἔπειτα ἑῷ ἐπέτελλεν ἕκαστος
ἵππους εὖ κατὰ κόσμον ἐρυκέμεν αὖθ’ ἐπὶ τάφρῳ·
sentences.l:
To his charioteer, then, his own, gave orders each man,
the horses well in due order to hold back there at the ditch,
sentences.i: Then each man ordered his own charioteer to hold the horses back there at the ditch, in good order,
sentences.n: These two lines are already in the poem, and the English is the one they have there. ἡνιόχῳ ‘to the charioteer’ is the person told, in the dative with ἐπέτελλεν, the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘give orders’. ἑῷ is the possessive ‘his own’ and ἕκαστος ‘each man’. ἐρυκέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’ (Attic ἐρύκειν). εὖ κατὰ κόσμον is ‘well in due order’, κόσμος being ‘order’. αὖθ’ is αὖθι ‘there, on the spot’. The charioteers keep the chariots at the ditch while the warriors go on.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ διαστάντες σφέας αὐτοὺς ἀρτύναντες
πένταχα κοσμηθέντες ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνεσσιν ἕποντο.
sentences.l:
and they, having stood apart, themselves having arrayed,
in five parts set in order, together with the leaders followed.
sentences.i: and they, standing apart and drawing themselves up, followed along with their leaders, set in order in five divisions.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ is ‘and they’, the Trojan warriors, now on foot. διαστάντες is the aorist participle of διίστημι ‘take up separate positions’. σφέας αὐτοὺς ἀρτύναντες ‘having arrayed themselves’ is the phrase of line 43, there used of the hunters. πένταχα is ‘in five parts’, an adverb in -χα, and κοσμηθέντες is the aorist passive participle of κοσμέω ‘set in order’; the Greek does not say here what the five are. ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνεσσιν is ‘together with leaders’, ἅμα with the epic dative plural, and ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’.
